```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A variable-order Markov chain describes a process in which the amount of
history needed to predict the next state depends on the history itself.
The model is stored as a prediction suffix tree: every node is a context, a
run of recent states, with a distribution over the next state, and a
context is kept only where the data support it (Ron, Singer, & Tishby,
1996; Bühlmann & Wyner, 1999). Fitting such a tree is one step of an
analysis that also has to decide how deep the tree may grow, which of its
contexts are reliable, how well it predicts data it has not seen, and
whether two groups of sequences differ.

This guide takes one event log through the whole analysis: reading the
data, fitting the tree, reading its pathways, smoothing and pruning,
choosing the depth by cross-validation, assessing fit, checking the
reliability of the pathways with the bootstrap, predicting next states,
and comparing two groups. Each step is treated briefly; the specialized
guides give the detail:
[data input](data-input.html),
[smoothing and pruning](smoothing-and-pruning.html),
[model selection](model-selection.html),
[pathway reliability](pathway-reliability.html),
[prediction and scoring](prediction-and-scoring.html),
[comparing groups](comparing-groups.html) and
[visualization](visualization.html).

```{r package}
library(transitiontrees)
```

## Data

`group_regulation_long` is an event log of collaborative regulation of
learning: each row is one regulation move made by a student working in a
small group. The data are synthetic, generated for the `tna` package from
its `group_regulation` data; they serve as a well-structured example and
are not evidence about students.

- **Actor:** `Actor`, the student; one sequence is built per student and
  session.
- **Time:** `Time`, the time stamp of the move (POSIXct), used to order the
  moves and to split sessions.
- **State:** `Action`, the regulation move, one of nine codes (`adapt`,
  `cohesion`, `consensus`, `coregulate`, `discuss`, `emotion`, `monitor`,
  `plan`, `synthesis`).
- **Group covariate:** `Achiever`, whether the student is a high or a low
  achiever; used in the group comparison.
- **Other columns:** `Group` (the collaboration group) and `Course`; not
  used here.

```{r data}
head(group_regulation_long)
with(group_regulation_long,
     c(events = length(Actor), students = length(unique(Actor)),
       groups = length(unique(Group)), courses = length(unique(Course))))
```

The log holds 27,533 moves by 2,000 students in 200 groups and three
courses.

## Fitting the tree

`context_tree()` reads the long log directly when the state column is
named in `action`. The moves of each `actor` are ordered by `time`, and a
gap of more than `time_threshold` seconds (default 900) starts a new
session. The tree below allows histories of up to three moves and gives a
context its own node when it occurs at least ten times.

```{r fit}
tree <- context_tree(group_regulation_long,
                     actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                     max_depth = 3, min_count = 10)
tree
```

The banner reports 2,000 sequences, one per student, and 27,533 observed
moves. The unpruned tree has 377 contexts. The first line of the tree is
the root, `(start)`: the next-move distribution with no history, in which
`consensus` is the most likely move with probability 0.25. Every deeper
context is judged against the prediction of its parent.

The root distribution is the marginal frequency of each move.

```{r frequencies}
state_frequencies(tree)
```

The moves are unevenly used: `consensus` and `plan` account for about a
quarter of the moves each, `adapt` and `synthesis` for 2% to 3%. A model
that always predicts `consensus` is correct a quarter of the time, so the
informative question is which histories change that default.

## Common and divergent pathways

The pathway tables give the contexts of the tree in one schema: the
pathway (oldest move on the left), its depth, its count, the most likely
next move and its probability, the Kullback-Leibler divergence in bits of
its next-move distribution from that of its parent, and whether the most
likely next move differs from the parent's (`changes_prediction`).
`common_pathways()` ranks the contexts by count.

```{r common}
common_pathways(tree, top = 8)
```

The most frequent histories are the single moves and the pairs formed by
`consensus` and `plan`. Their divergences are small at depth 2: after
`consensus -> plan` the next move is predicted almost exactly as after
`plan` alone (0.0006 bits). `divergent_pathways()` ranks by divergence
instead.

```{r divergent}
divergent_pathways(tree, top = 8)
```

Six of the eight most divergent contexts are three-move histories seen
10 to 19 times, close to the minimum of ten that the fit allows. After
`consensus -> cohesion -> plan`, for example, `plan` follows with
probability 0.83, against 0.36 after `cohesion -> plan`, but the estimate rests
on 12 occurrences. A large divergence on a small count is the pattern that
pruning and the bootstrap are designed to test: it may reflect a real
routine or a handful of sequences.

## Smoothing and pruning

Each node carries a smoothed distribution; the default `floor` smoother
leaves a fully observed distribution unchanged and gives every unobserved
next move a probability of 0.001. Pruning then removes the contexts whose
history does not change the prediction of the parent by more than chance.
`compare_pruning()` applies the four criteria to the same tree.

```{r compare-pruning}
compare_pruning(tree)
```

The likelihood-ratio criterion `G2` keeps 23 of the 377 contexts; `AIC`
keeps 20 and `BIC` 10, while `KL`, at its default threshold of 0.005
nats, keeps almost all of them. Most of the grown depth is therefore not
supported. The tree pruned with `G2` at $\alpha = 0.05$ is used below.

```{r prune}
pruned <- prune_tree(tree, criterion = "G2", alpha = 0.05)
pruned
```

The pruned tree keeps the root, the nine single moves and 13 longer
histories. [Smoothing and pruning](smoothing-and-pruning.html) gives the
formulas of the five smoothers and four criteria.

## Choosing the depth by cross-validation

In-sample criteria reward deeper trees. `tune_tree()` estimates the
predictive quality of each configuration on data the tree has not seen: it
divides the sequences into `folds` groups, fits on all but one, and
computes the perplexity of the held-out group. The grid below crosses
three depths with pruned and unpruned trees.

```{r tune}
tuning <- tune_tree(group_regulation_long,
                    actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                    max_depth = 1:3, min_count = 10, prune = c(FALSE, TRUE),
                    folds = 5, seed = 1)
summary(tuning)
as.data.frame(tuning, what = "grid")
```

The lowest held-out perplexity, 5.46, belongs to the first-order tree.
The pruned trees of depth 2 and 3 are within 0.03 of it, whereas the
unpruned depth-3 tree reaches 5.88: without pruning, the deeper contexts
fit noise that does not recur in new sequences. For predicting the next
move, one move of history is enough in these data; the longer contexts that
survive pruning add little predictive accuracy, although they may still be
of substantive interest. [Model selection](model-selection.html) covers
the tuning grid, the information criteria and the stability of the
selection across fold assignments.

## Assessing fit

`model_fit()` returns the log likelihood, the number of free parameters
`df` (the number of contexts times the number of states minus one), the
number of predicted moves, AIC, BIC and perplexity in one row.

```{r fit-scalars}
rbind(unpruned = model_fit(tree), pruned = model_fit(pruned))
```

The unpruned tree has the higher in-sample likelihood and the lower
in-sample perplexity (5.21 against 5.43), but it spends 3,016 parameters
to obtain them; both AIC and BIC favor the pruned tree with 184
parameters. The in-sample perplexity of the pruned tree is close to its
held-out value in the tuning grid (5.49), which indicates that it does not
overfit.

## Reliability of the pathways

A context retained by pruning has passed a test in this sample.
`bootstrap_pathways()` asks whether it would pass again: it resamples whole
sequences with replacement, refits the tree on each resample, and reports
for each pathway whether its count is stable and whether its likelihood
ratio statistic against its parent exceeds the critical value in most
resamples.

```{r bootstrap}
boot <- bootstrap_pathways(pruned, iter = 200, seed = 1)
boot
```

Of the 23 pathways of the pruned tree, 22 are stable and 14 informative;
13 are both: the nine single moves and four
longer histories. `as.data.frame()` returns the bootstrap estimates of
every pathway with percentile intervals; the longer histories are:

```{r bootstrap-table}
subset(as.data.frame(boot, what = "summary"), depth > 1,
       select = c(pathway, count, stable, informative, informative_rate,
                  ci_G2_lo, ci_G2_hi))
```

The four longer histories that are both stable and informative are
`discuss -> coregulate -> discuss`, `emotion -> emotion -> consensus`,
`adapt -> discuss` and `cohesion -> cohesion`; their likelihood ratio
statistic exceeds the critical value of 15.5 in 84% to 96% of the
resamples. These are the contexts on which a claim about longer memory can
rest. The divergent `consensus -> cohesion -> plan` is retained by pruning
and its count is stable, but its statistic exceeds the critical value in
only 64% of the resamples, so its departure from `cohesion -> plan` is not
reproducible.

[Pathway reliability](pathway-reliability.html) describes the two criteria
and the distribution of the resampled statistics.

## Predicting the next move

`predict()` applies the longest-suffix rule: the prediction for a history
is the distribution of the longest context in the tree that ends the
history. With `tidy = TRUE` it returns one row per history with the
matched context, the most likely next move and the full distribution.

```{r predict}
histories <- list(c("plan", "consensus"),
                  c("discuss", "coregulate", "discuss"),
                  "monitor")
predict(pruned, newdata = histories, tidy = TRUE)
```

The first history is predicted from `consensus` alone, because the pruned
tree holds no longer context ending in it; the second matches the full
three-move context retained by pruning. [Prediction and
scoring](prediction-and-scoring.html) covers scoring of whole sequences,
imputation and the generation of new sequences.

## Comparing high and low achievers

Naming the external grouping column in `group` fits one tree per group
over a shared alphabet. The comparison uses depth 2, so that most contexts
are observed often enough in both groups.

```{r groups}
groups <- context_tree(group_regulation_long,
                       actor = "Actor", time = "Time", action = "Action",
                       group = "Achiever", max_depth = 2, min_count = 10)
summary(groups)
```

Each group contributes 1,000 sequences, with 13,721 and 13,812 moves;
the two trees have 74 and 77 contexts. `compare_groups()` tests two kinds of
difference by permuting the group labels of whole sequences: whether,
after the same history, the groups choose different next moves
(`behavioral`, a count-weighted Jensen-Shannon divergence), and whether
they reach the same histories at the same rates (`usage`, a G-squared
homogeneity statistic).

```{r compare-groups}
comparison <- compare_groups(groups, iter = 99, seed = 1)
summary(comparison)
```

Both omnibus statistics exceed every one of the 99 permuted values
(p = 0.01, the smallest attainable with 99 permutations), so high and low
achievers differ both in what they do after a given history and in which
histories they reach. The contexts ranked by behavioral divergence, with
Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values:

```{r compare-pathways}
head(as.data.frame(comparison, what = "pathways"))
```

[Comparing groups](comparing-groups.html) explains the two statistics, the
stratified permutation for nested data and the plots of group differences.

## Reporting

A report of this analysis states the data and session rule, the fitted and
selected configurations, and the evidence for each claim, for example:

> Regulation moves were modeled as a variable-order Markov chain with a
> prediction suffix tree (Ron, Singer, & Tishby, 1996). Moves were grouped
> into one sequence per student and session (gap > 900 s), giving 2,000
> sequences and 27,533 moves over nine codes. A tree of depth 3 (contexts
> observed at least ten times; floor smoothing, $y_{\min} = 0.001$) was
> pruned by likelihood-ratio tests at $\alpha = 0.05$, which retained 23
> of 377 contexts. Five-fold cross-validation favored one move of history
> (held-out perplexity 5.46; pruned depth 3: 5.49). In 200 bootstrap
> resamples, 13 pathways were stable and informative, four of them
> longer than one move. High and low achievers differed in next-move
> choices given the same history and in the histories they reached
> (permutation tests with 99 permutations, both p = 0.01).
